## Role and Scope

The balance of plant (BOP) includes the non-electrical auxiliary equipment required to operate the PEM electrolyser stack safely and continuously. In this model, the BOP manages feedwater supply, heat removal, gas-liquid separation, hydrogen drying, hydrogen-side piping, instrumentation and housing.

Because the system is offshore, the feedwater system must also include seawater intake, desalination and final purification to electrolyser-grade water.

Power electronics are excluded completely because the required components depend on the electrical architecture. Transformers, rectifiers and other electrical conversion equipment are discussed on [Electrolyser Power Electronics](elx_power_electronics.qmd).

The stack, compressors, hydrogen export system, offshore installation, offshore structures and indirect project costs are also represented elsewhere in the model.

The scope used in this page is therefore:

| Included in this BOP model          | Excluded from this BOP model        |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Thermal management                  | PEM electrolyser stack              |
| Feedwater handling                  | Power electronics                   |
| Seawater intake                     | Transformers and rectifiers         |
| Desalination and final purification | Hydrogen compression                |
| Gas-liquid separation               | Hydrogen export system              |
| Hydrogen drying                     | Offshore foundations and structures |
| Hydrogen-side BOP piping            | Offshore installation               |
| Instrumentation and housing         | Site preparation and indirect costs |

: Scope boundary for the balance-of-plant model.

## Reference purchase cost

The model returns one aggregate BOP equipment purchase cost in EUR~2025~.
Internal stack-water handling is included in that aggregate; desalination is
not a separate cost-ledger item. Installation, platforms, compression, stack
purchase and power electronics remain outside this boundary.

### Inputs and reference basis

| Input | Adopted value | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| NREL source rating | {{< var bop-source-rating >}} | Modular PEM system [@badgett2024PEMCost, Table 10] |
| Aggregate reference rating | {{< var bop-reference-rating >}} | Adopted turbine-scale cost anchor |
| Reference-building exponent | {{< var bop-reference-build-exponent >}} | DNV BOP scaling applied from the NREL rating to the adopted anchor [@dnv2023OffshoreHydrogen, section 3.2.1] |
| Downstream BOP exponent | {{< var bop-scaling-exponent >}} | Adopted for the whole package; same DNV basis |
| Maximum BOP block rating | {{< var bop-block-limit >}} | Retained screening bound, not supplier qualification |
| Thermal water-treatment allowance | {{< var bop-water-treatment-unit-cost >}} | DNV supplier indication; EUR2023 is an explicit price-year assumption [@dnv2023OffshoreHydrogen, Table 3-3] |
| Manufacturer markup | {{< var hydrogen-manufactured-cost-markup >}} | Applied to NREL manufactured costs only [@badgett2024PEMCost] |

All fixed inputs are stored in `model_data/inputs.csv`. The calculation is owned
by `model/hydrogen_production/balance_of_plant.py`; the website and case runner
use its `reference_cost_basis` result.

### Build the aggregate reference

The NREL manufacturing-output case is 1,000 MW/year. Its non-electrical BOP
includes the following categories [@badgett2024PEMCost, Table 10]:

| Category | Manufactured cost, USD2020/kW |
|---|---:|
| Water supply, including internal water handling | {{< var bop-water-supply-manufactured-unit-cost-value >}} |
| Thermal management | {{< var bop-thermal-manufactured-unit-cost-value >}} |
| Hydrogen processing | {{< var bop-processing-manufactured-unit-cost-value >}} |
| Hydrogen-side BOP | {{< var bop-hydrogen-side-manufactured-unit-cost-value >}} |
| Piping, instrumentation and housing | {{< var bop-piping-housing-manufactured-unit-cost-value >}} |
| **Calculated total** | **{{< var bop-cost-source-manufactured-usd2020-per-kw >}}** |

Water supply is retained in full. It includes feedwater treatment, the feed tank,
polishing, filtration and recirculation equipment [@badgett2024PEMCost, section
2.2.1 and Table 3]. The DEA increment is interpreted as thermal seawater
desalination upstream of this existing water-handling scope. No extra internal
water-handling charge or cooling credit is applied. This is a screening boundary:
the supplier breakdown is insufficient to verify all heat-exchanger and
purification interfaces, so overlap must be checked when package evidence improves.

For source rating $P_0$ [kW], summed manufactured unit cost $c_0$ [USD2020/kW],
markup multiplier $M$ [-], USD escalation $I_\mathrm{US}$ [-] and exchange rate
$X$ [USD/EUR], the source purchase cost is

$$
C_{0,2025}=c_0P_0M I_\mathrm{US}/X.
$$

The [common price method](../methodology/financial_and_price_basis.qmd) supplies
$I_\mathrm{US}$ and $X$. The calculated source purchase cost is
**{{< var bop-cost-source-purchase-eur2025 >}} EUR2025**.

Scale this existing BOP to the adopted reference rating $P_r$ [kW] using the
reference-building exponent $\alpha_r$ [-]:

$$
C_{\mathrm{process},r}=C_{0,2025}(P_r/P_0)^{\alpha_r}.
$$

This gives **{{< var bop-cost-process-reference-eur2025 >}} EUR2025**.
The source category costs are not multiplied linearly by the larger reference rating.

DNV's thermal treatment coefficient $u_w$ [EUR2023/MW] anchors the additional
allowance at the same rating:

$$
C_{w,r,2023}=u_w(P_r/1000),\qquad
C_{w,r,2025}=C_{w,r,2023}(1+h_{2024})(1+h_{2025}).
$$

The division by 1000 converts kW to MW. The source-basis allowance is
**{{< var bop-cost-water-reference-eur2023 >}} EUR2023**.
DNV does not establish the quote's price year. Treating it as the report-year
EUR2023 is an adopted screening exception, not sourced price-year evidence.
The euro-area annual HICP rates $h_{2024}$ =
{{< var platform-benchmark-hicp-2024 >}} and $h_{2025}$ =
{{< var platform-benchmark-hicp-2025 >}} are reused from the shared input table
[@eurostat2026AnnualHICP]. Consumer inflation is a fallback rather than an
equipment-specific index. The derived escalation factor is
{{< var bop-cost-water-escalation-factor >}}, giving
**{{< var bop-cost-water-reference-eur2025 >}} EUR2025**. No manufacturer markup
is added to the DEA supplier allowance, and its separately listed installation
percentage is not added to purchase cost.

Finally,

$$
C_{\mathrm{BOP},r}=C_{\mathrm{process},r}+C_{w,r,2025}.
$$

The aggregate reference is **{{< var bop-cost-aggregate-reference-eur2025 >}}
EUR2025**. These contributions explain the reference; the model books their sum
once as BOP.

## Scaling method {#scaling-method}

For wind capacity served at one production location $P$ [kW], maximum block
rating $P_{\max}$ [kW], block count $n_b$ [-] and block rating $P_i$ [kW]:

$$
n_b=\left\lceil P/P_{\max}\right\rceil,\qquad
P_i=P/n_b,\qquad
C_{\mathrm{BOP,location}}=n_b C_{\mathrm{BOP},r}(P_i/P_r)^\alpha.
$$

Sum these costs across production locations. Centralised production shares
farm capacity across blocks; distributed production sizes blocks at each turbine.
Stack overplanting does not resize BOP. No spare block is included.

The baseline exponent $\alpha$ is {{< var bop-scaling-exponent >}}.
DNV proposes this exponent for BOP, while listing thermal treatment separately
[@dnv2023OffshoreHydrogen, sections 3.2.1 and 3.3]. Applying it to the entire
aggregate, including water treatment, is the adopted modelling assumption.
The DEA linear allowance is used only to establish the reference, not reapplied
at each block rating.

Retain 0.6 as an explicit sensitivity override of `bop-scaling-exponent`.
The reference-building exponent remains unchanged, preserving the same reference
cost in both cases. Scenario result input records retain the baseline and applied
override. This tests economies of scale without changing the turbine-scale anchor.

## BOP Power Consumption

The BOP also consumes electricity during electrolyser operation. This consumption is treated separately from stack electricity consumption.

The BOP power consumption represents parasitic loads from auxiliary systems such as pumps, fans, chillers, recirculation blowers, thermal management and hydrogen drying.

Compression is excluded from this value because compression is represented elsewhere in the model. Electrical conversion losses are also explicitly excluded because power electronics are represented separately.

The NREL report cites a generic BOP electricity consumption of 4.2 kWh/kg H₂ (Table 1), but this value includes electrical losses and is therefore not directly applicable to the non-electrical BOP scope used here [@badgett2024PEMCost].

The underlying Ruth and Ahluwalia source [@badgett2024PEMCost] separates BOP losses into electrical, mechanical and hydrogen-related losses. After excluding electrical losses, the remaining BOP consumption is:

| Operating point         | Mechanical [kWh/kg H₂] | Hydrogen [kWh/kg H₂] | Total [kWh/kg H₂] |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------: | -------------------: | ----------------: |
| Rated power, BOL        |                    1.3 |                  0.2 |               1.5 |
| Rated power, EOL        |                    2.3 |                  0.2 |               2.5 |
| Minimum-loss point, BOL |                    0.4 |                  0.1 |               0.5 |
| Minimum-loss point, EOL |                    0.6 |                  0.1 |               0.7 |

: Non-electrical BOP electricity consumption after excluding electrical losses.

A simple lifetime average gives approximately 2.0 kWh/kg H₂ at rated power and 0.6 kWh/kg H₂ at the minimum-loss operating point. The difference is mainly caused by thermal management. At the minimum-loss operating point, the stack operates more efficiently and therefore produces less waste heat. Lower waste heat reduces the cooling duty and associated mechanical power consumption.

In this study, the stack is deliberately oversized so that the electrolyser usually operates closer to the minimum-loss point than to rated stack operation. The model therefore assumes an average non-electrical BOP power consumption of:

$$
e_\mathrm{BOP} = 1.0 \ \mathrm{kWh/kg_{H_2}}
$$

This value includes mechanical BOP loads and hydrogen drying losses. It is selected as a conservative average. It is higher than the minimum-loss values reported by Ruth and Ahluwalia to allow for offshore cooling, water handling, drying, control systems, part-load operation and uncertainty in auxiliary loads.

### Water-treatment integration

The adopted DEA cost evidence assumes thermal desalination using electrolyser
waste heat [@dnv2023OffshoreHydrogen, section 3.3]. The existing aggregate BOP
electricity allowance is retained; no separate desalination electrical load is
added. This is not a verified thermal balance. **TODO:** establish usable heat
at the operating temperatures and part-load states of the oversized stack,
treatment duty and buffering, and check the aggregate auxiliary allowance.
Failure to provide sufficient heat would require a different treatment design
and cost basis, rather than assuming free supplementary heat.

The total BOP electricity consumption is calculated as:

$$
E_\mathrm{BOP} = e_\mathrm{BOP} \cdot m_\mathrm{H_2}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{BOP}$ is the BOP electricity consumption and $m_\mathrm{H_2}$ is the hydrogen production.

The assumed value of $e_\mathrm{BOP}$ should be interpreted as an average value for an oversized offshore PEM electrolyser operating predominantly away from rated stack power.

## Model limitations

- The NREL source describes an onshore modular system. Scaling it to the adopted
  reference and then to shared blocks is a screening approximation.
- Internal water handling remains within BOP. The DEA increment assumes upstream
  thermal desalination; supplier evidence must resolve purification and cooling
  interfaces before claiming a fully reconciled equipment inventory.
- Thermal integration and auxiliary consumption require validation at the actual
  stack operating conditions. The cost allowance does not demonstrate feasibility.
- The DEA quote year is assumed, and HICP is a broad price-index proxy.
- Aggregate scaling omits treatment-package thresholds and redundancy. The retained
  block limit bounds centralisation benefits but is not engineering qualification.
- Offshore intake scope, integration and installation remain unresolved; no zero
  costs are inferred. Offshore installation belongs to its owning campaign model.

The workflow exposes `physical.bop_purchase_cost_basis` for auditing the source
subtotal, reference contributions, price conversion and aggregate reference.
